Troop 513 Advancement Dashboard

Advancement Trends

Time in current rank vs the troop's typical step

Days since each scout earned their latest rank, compared with the troop median for that step. Over the pace (red) means longer than the median. Pace risk (yellow) means within 30 days before the median. Within pace (green) is earlier than that. Scouts with no earlier history for that step show no comparison. The last two columns show how close each scout is to the next rank and when anything was last entered for them.

Average time between ranks

Days from earning one rank to earning the next (date earned in Scoutbook). Bars are averages; the tick marks the median; the thin line spans fastest to slowest. The last bar is the whole Scout to First Class stretch.

Scout to First Class: last 10 scouts

Time each scout took from earning Scout to earning First Class, for the scouts who earned First Class most recently, newest first. Green bars took the troop average or less; yellow bars took longer. The dashed line is the troop average for every scout who has earned First Class.

Rank advancements per quarter

Ranks earned in each of the last 12 quarters.

Pace by the year a scout earned Scout

Average days to First Class for each class of new scouts, and how many have finished.

Merit badges earned

Badges completed per year, and the scouts with the most (Eagle-required in the lighter segment). Troop leaders often enter badges in batches (for example 90 on 2026-08-09 and 65 on 2026-02-26), so yearly bars show when badges were recorded more than when they were earned.
Dates come from Scoutbook rank records (date earned). Ranks with no date are left out; averages only include scouts who have both ranks. Contains minors' names and progress: share only with named people.

How to Use This Dashboard

A guided tour of every page: what it is for, how to use it, and what to watch out for. Start with the basics below, then open the tab for any page. Words you do not know are on the Definitions tab. The pictures show made-up sample scouts and patrols, so no real names appear on this page.

Basics
Dashboard pages

Start here

This dashboard turns the troop's Scoutbook advancement records into pages that answer practical questions: who is close to a rank, who has gone quiet, what to teach this week, and who has something to present at the next Court of Honor. You can only look. Nothing you click here changes anything in Scoutbook.

Where the numbers come from

A snapshot of the troop's Scoutbook records, pulled once a day. The line at the top of every page says when. If it is more than a day and a half old, a yellow warning appears and the numbers may be behind what has been entered since.

Who is included

Only the active scouts. The top line also names the excluded patrol, the one Scoutbook uses for inactive scouts, which is left out of every page.

Fixing a number

If a record looks wrong, correct it in Scoutbook. The change shows up here after the next daily update.

Nothing is saved

Filters, limits and choices you make reset when you reload the page. The one exception is the Book Checked marks on , which are kept in the page address.

Getting around

Use the Sections button at the top left to move between pages. The line under the title always shows which page you are on.

  • Click a scout's name wherever it is a blue link to open that scout in . On a name opens that scout's checklist instead. Names are written Last, First so that lists read like a roster.
  • Click a column title to sort a table. Click it again to reverse the order. The arrow beside the title shows which column is sorted and in which direction.
  • Filter boxes above a table narrow what it shows, and a line such as "Showing 12 of 24 scouts" tells you how many rows are left. Clear a box to see everyone again.
  • Colored cards that look like buttons (for example on ) filter the table when you click them. Click again to clear the filter.
  • Hover over a requirement number to read the requirement. On a phone or tablet, tap it, and tap it again to hide it. Escape hides it too.
  • An arrow (▸) before a card or row means it can be opened. Many pages also have Expand all and Collapse all buttons.
  • On a phone, tables turn into stacked cards and a Sort by menu replaces the column titles.

Which page answers my question?

Find your question, then open that page or read how to use it. Every page also has its own tab at the top of this guide, in the same order as the Sections menu (on a phone, use the menu in its place). Each has a picture, steps and things worth knowing. Click or tap a picture to see it at full size.

The scouts and patrols in this guide (such as Alex Sample and Sample Patrol Alpha) are made up. The dashboard itself shows the troop's real scouts and contains the names and progress of minors, so share it only with people who should see the whole troop.

Definitions

Words and phrases that appear on more than one page.

Next rank
The lowest rank a scout has not completed yet. Most pages work from the open requirements for it.
Open requirement
A requirement that is not marked complete in Scoutbook.
Final steps
The Scoutmaster conference, the board of review, Scout spirit and the parent exercises. A scout whose only open items are final steps is ready for a conference and board.
Looks met
A requirement whose dates and logs in Scoutbook already show it is done, but that nobody has signed off yet. A leader still has to sign it off in Scoutbook.
Clock
A requirement that takes time to pass (for example 30 days or 4 months), or a rank that needs time in rank. Starting a clock early is the only way to speed it up.
Book Checked
A button on . Press it after you compare a scout's handbook with Scoutbook, and their age restarts from today until something newer is entered.
Over the pace, Pace risk, Within pace
How long a scout has held their current rank compared with the troop's median for that step: longer than the median, within 30 days before it (or at it), or earlier than that. See .
Eagle clock and slack
Months until a scout turns 18, minus the months the minimum timeline still needs (time in rank and positions of responsibility). Slack is what is left over, and short means the minimum timeline no longer fits. See .
Position of responsibility
A troop leadership role, such as patrol leader, that Star, Life and Eagle each require a scout to hold for a number of months.
Station
A short meeting activity, 10 to 60 minutes, that recommends running so that several scouts check off requirements at once.
Recorded and done
On , the date recorded is when the sign-off was entered in Scoutbook. When the scout did the work earlier, the earlier date is shown as done.
Court of Honor (COH)
The troop ceremony where ranks and merit badges are presented. lists what was earned since the last one.

Overview

The landing page. It pulls the most useful numbers from the other pages onto one screen so you can see at a glance who needs attention and where to look next. Everything on it is a shortcut: click a number, a scout's name or a link ending in › to open the page behind it.

How to use it

  1. Check the line at the top of the dashboard first. It says when the data was pulled from Scoutbook, and a yellow warning appears when the data is more than a day and a half old.
  2. Read the six tiles: records over the red limit, scouts ready for a conference or board, scouts over the typical pace, scouts on the Star to Eagle trail, merit badges in progress, and scouts with 20 or more camping nights. The small line under each number adds detail.
  3. Click a tile to open the page behind it. Click a scout's name in any panel to open that scout in .
  4. Scan the six panels for the scouts that need attention, and use the link in a panel's corner to open the full page.
  5. Finish with the strip at the bottom: where the troop is by rank, and how much has been signed off recently.

Good to know

  • The numbers follow the settings you change on other pages: the yellow and red limits and Book Checked marks on , the Eagle clock warning on , the goal on , and the attendance, program time and pace switch on .
  • ready for conference or board counts every scout whose only open items are final steps (Scoutmaster conference, board of review, Scout spirit and the parent exercises). The Hold first line in the meeting panel only counts scouts marked as coming on This Week's Meeting.
  • Most common gaps leaves out the final steps that every scout still has, so what is left are requirements you can actually teach.
  • Closest to the next rank also shows each scout's top next step, the same first priority you would see in Scout Detail.
  • The sign-off counts count requirements, not scouts.

Rank Update Aging

Shows how long it has been since each scout last had a rank requirement marked complete in Scoutbook, so you can find records that have gone quiet. A long gap can mean a scout is stuck, or that work they did was never entered.

How to use it

  1. Look at the colored cards for the big picture, and click one to see only those scouts.
  2. Set the Yellow threshold (days) and Red threshold (days) to how often you want records updated. They start at 30 and 90.
  3. Narrow the list with Scout (a name in either order), Patrol, Current rank, Min days and Max days (for example 31 to 60) and Last requirement (a rank, a requirement number or a keyword).
  4. Click a column title to sort the table. Hover over a requirement number in Last updated requirement to read it.
  5. After you review a scout's book against Scoutbook, press Book Checked. The age restarts from today and the row says book checked. Undo takes it back, and a newer sign-off in Scoutbook takes over on its own.

Good to know

  • The date is the latest completed, marked-complete or leader-approved date on a rank requirement, so it can be the day a requirement was entered or approved rather than the day the work was done. Merit badge sign-offs never reset it. If a scout has only rank dates, the row says (rank marked complete).
  • Book Checked marks are kept only in the address of the page you opened (the part after the #), so they belong to that browser and link. Opening the dashboard from a fresh link starts without them.
  • The page counts days to today's date on the device you are using. counts to the date the data was pulled, so the two can differ by a day or more.
  • Keep Yellow lower than Red. Otherwise the amber card is empty and its label reads backwards.
  • Split the red list by Patrol or Current rank to hand it out for follow-up, and glance at the header first: an old snapshot makes everything look staler than it is.

Overall Missing Reqs

Shows which Scout through First Class requirements the most scouts still need, and who they are. Use it to decide what to teach next: the requirement at the top of the list helps the most scouts at once.

How to use it

  1. Read the four rank cards, which count the scouts who still need each rank. Click one to show only that rank, and click it again to clear it.
  2. Under Biggest gaps across the troop, click a button to jump straight to that requirement.
  3. Narrow the table with Rank, Requirement contains (a keyword or a requirement number) and Min scouts. Raise Min scouts to hide gaps that only one or two scouts have.
  4. Click a row to open it. Last signed off in the troop shows the most recent sign-off, and Scouts who still need this lists everyone who is missing it.
  5. Click a column title to sort. The table starts with the requirement that the most scouts are missing.

Good to know

  • Scouts with no record yet for a rank are counted as needing every requirement of that rank. Their names appear with a dashed outline and rank not started.
  • Every incomplete rank counts for each scout, not just the next one. A Tenderfoot scout is also counted under Second Class and First Class requirements.
  • An old Last signed off in the troop date means nobody has finished that requirement lately. It looks at every scout with a record, including scouts who already finished the rank, and matches requirements by number and wording.
  • The numbers on the rank cards match the counts on . The Overview's Most common gaps panel shows the same rows, minus the final steps every scout still has.

Rank-By-Rank Detail

Looks at one rank at a time (Scout, Tenderfoot, Second Class or First Class) and shows who is still working on it, how far along each scout is, and which requirements are still open. Use it to plan a session for scouts working on the same rank.

How to use it

  1. Choose a rank with the buttons at the top.
  2. Read the cards and the list Scouts still working on... to see who is closest to finishing and how many requirements each scout has open.
  3. Under Requirements and who still needs them, find the requirement that the most scouts need and see exactly who they are.
  4. Narrow the table with Requirement contains, Scout contains and Min scouts, and click a column title to sort. Your filters stay in place when you switch to another rank.

Good to know

  • Scouts that Scoutbook has no record for yet on this rank are marked (not started) and count as needing every requirement.
  • The percent is Scoutbook's own figure for the rank, not the number of open requirements.
  • Scout contains looks at the name written as "Last, First", so type just a first or last name. It narrows the table but not the cards or the list of scouts.
  • To plan a group session, pick a rank and look at the top of the table: those are the requirements the most of those scouts still need. does this grouping for you.

Star Life Eagle Trail

Tracks the scouts working toward Star, Life or Eagle. Scoutbook only shows each requirement as done or not done; this page adds the clocks behind them: time in rank, merit badge counts, service hours since the last rank, and positions of responsibility. You can see what is waiting on time, what is waiting on work, and what already looks met but is not signed off.

How to use it

  1. Read the cards at the top: how many scouts are on the trail, how many have requirements that look met, who needs a position of responsibility to start the clock, and who is inside the Eagle clock warning.
  2. Use Working toward to see only Star, Life or Eagle scouts, and set Eagle clock warning (months of slack) to the amount of slack at which you want an early warning.
  3. Read across a scout's row: how complete the rank is in Scoutbook, Time in rank, Merit badges, Service hours, Position and Eagle clock. Green means met, amber means waiting, and red means there is no current position.
  4. The table starts with the scouts who have the least Eagle clock slack. Click a column title to sort another way.
  5. Click a scout's name to open their checklist under the table. It lists every open requirement with what the numbers say about it.

Good to know

  • Looks met comes from the dates and logs in Scoutbook. It does not replace a leader's sign-off: someone still has to sign the requirement off in Scoutbook.
  • The rules built in: Star needs 4 months as First Class, 6 merit badges (4 Eagle-required) and 6 service hours. Life needs 6 months as Star, 11 badges (7 Eagle-required) and 6 service hours. Eagle needs 6 months as Life and 21 badges including every Eagle-required slot. A position of responsibility must be held for the same number of months.
  • The Eagle clock counts only time in rank and positions, not badges, service, the Eagle project or paperwork. N mo short in red means the minimum timeline no longer fits before age 18. over 4 years away appears when the scout is far from 18 or no birth date is recorded; birth dates are never shown on the page.
  • Only the positions the requirement lists count (assistant patrol leader does not), and only while they are held. No position now means that clock is not running yet.
  • uses the same numbers for each scout's top priorities, and the Overview shows this page's tightest scouts.

Scout Detail

Everything about one scout on a single screen: where they are on the rank ladder, how recently anything was entered for them, what is still open for their next rank, which merit badges they have started, and the few things most worth doing next.

How to use it

  1. Choose a scout in the Scout list, or use the arrow buttons beside it to step through the troop in order.
  2. Read the rank ladder and the five cards for the quick picture: how recent the last update was, which rank they hold, how close the next rank is, how many merit badges are in progress and how many nights they have camped.
  3. Read Top priority (or Top 3 priorities). These are picked from the open requirements and the clocks that need time to pass: sign-offs that already look met and clocks that should be started come first, then activities that check off several requirements at once.
  4. For a Star, Life or Eagle scout, read the Eagle clock line under the priorities. It says how many months are left before 18 and how much slack the minimum timeline leaves.
  5. Scroll down to Missing requirements for the next rank and the Active merit badges. Click a badge to unfold its open requirements, and hover over a requirement number to read it.

Good to know

  • The first card is colored with the yellow and red limits from , so amber or red means nothing has been entered lately. It ignores Book Checked marks.
  • The priority labels tell you what kind of step it is: Ready now (only the conference, board, Scout spirit or parent items are left: book them), Needs sign-off (the numbers already look met, so a leader only has to approve it), Start the clock (the requirement needs weeks or months), Clock not running (a position of responsibility is needed) and Do together (one activity checks off several requirements).
  • The 20-night camping goal on this page is fixed. It does not follow the goal box on , and the Eagle clock line is never colored.
  • The Eagle clock line is left out when no birth date is recorded or the scout is more than 4 years from 18.
  • You can also get here by clicking a scout's name on the Overview or on .

Incomplete Merit Badges

Lists every merit badge that scouts have started but not finished, who is working on each one, and which requirements are still open. Use it to find badges to push over the line, or requirements several scouts need at once.

How to use it

  1. Read the four tiles for the troop-wide picture.
  2. Under Closest to finishing, click a button to jump to that scout's badge. The scouts nearest the finish are listed first.
  3. Narrow the cards with Merit badge or Scout, and choose Sort by: Most scouts, Closest to finishing or Badge name. Expand all and Collapse all open or close every card.
  4. Click a badge's card to see each scout working on it, with a progress bar and how many requirements are open, and the requirements themselves.

Good to know

  • When two or more scouts work on a badge, the card separates Every scout still needs from Only some scouts need. The first list is what a single group session could cover.
  • A card's bar shows the average progress of its scouts, and the text beside it also gives the best progress. Requirements of the kind "choose 2 of 3" count as one open item.
  • Typing a name in Scout keeps only that scout's badges and recalculates the card numbers. The tiles and the Closest to finishing buttons always show the whole troop.
  • Only badges that a scout has started in Scoutbook appear here.
  • The Overview's merit badges in progress tile counts scout-badge pairs and opens this page.

30-Day Personal Plan

A to-do plan for one scout. It shows the activities that would check off the most of their open requirements for their next rank, which of those can be done together in one outing or meeting, and what would still be left over. It uses the same activity ideas as , but for one scout at a time.

How to use it

  1. Choose a scout in the Scout list. The arrow buttons step through the troop.
  2. Read the four cards: how complete the next rank is, how many open requirements the ideas can check off, how many need time to pass, and whether the scout is ready for a conference and board after the plan.
  3. Look at On a campout and At troop meetings. Each shows up to three idea cards, best first. A green at once tag means the idea checks off two or more requirements together.
  4. Open How to run it on a card for the steps and a tip.
  5. Scroll down to Everything else still open: Start the clock now, Do at home with a parent, Final steps and Still to plan, each with a count.
  6. Tick Include swimming and boating ideas only if you have a pool or waterfront.

Good to know

  • Start with Start the clock now: requirements tagged takes ... (for example 30 days or 6 months) cannot be rushed, so an early start helps. The page recognizes a wait only when the requirement spells out a number of days, weeks or months.
  • The campout ideas are chosen first, and the meeting ideas then cover what the campout does not.
  • The page does not set dates; it shows what to do and what has to be started early.
  • Do at home with a parent items are the parent exercises, which a scout does with a parent rather than at a meeting.
  • Star, Life and Eagle scouts get few ideas, because the activity list mostly covers requirements up through First Class. is the better page for them.
  • The swimming box here is separate from the one on Activity Ideas.

Activity Ideas

Suggests the activities that would move the most scouts toward their next rank at once. A list of 22 ready-made ideas (9 for a camping trip and 13 for a troop meeting) is matched against every scout's open requirements, and the best ones are picked for a campout and for a meeting.

How to use it

  1. Read the note at the top for how ideas are scored, then look at the two blocks separately: On a camping trip and At a regular troop meeting.
  2. In each block, start with idea #1. Each card gives a short pitch, how many scouts it helps and how many requirements it checks off, and What to do.
  3. Read Requirements it checks off. It lists each requirement, with a number showing how many scouts still need it. These are the sign-offs to give afterwards.
  4. Open Scouts who benefit to see who to invite and how close each scout is to finishing the rank.
  5. Tick Include swimming and boating ideas only if you have a pool or waterfront.

Good to know

  • Picks are chosen one at a time, so each idea adds the most beyond the ones before it. The line If you run all three counts the three together, with each scout counted once.
  • Every scout with a next rank counts; there is no attendance filter here. Use to plan around who is actually coming.
  • To build the next campout, start with card #1 of the camping block and invite the scouts under Scouts who benefit.
  • Few ideas cover Star, Life and Eagle requirements.
  • The same ideas and scoring drive the , the Do together cards in , and .

Camping Nights

Tracks each scout's camping nights against a goal (20 nights, the Camping merit badge requirement) and checks the recent troop trips against each scout's Scoutbook book. Use it to see who is behind and to find trips whose nights were never entered.

How to use it

  1. Read the cards at the top, then the Trips to double-check buttons. Hover over a trip to see why it was flagged.
  2. Set Goal (nights) and Trips from (the last 12, 24 or 36 months, or all time) if you want something other than 20 nights and 24 months. Filter by Scout or Patrol and choose how to order the cards with Sort cards by.
  3. Under Scouts under 20 nights, the scouts furthest from the goal come first. Open a card (the first one is open) to see the scout's nights, how many come from the troop trips below, and each recent trip marked as in or out of their book.
  4. Scroll down to the table of scouts who have reached the goal. Click a column title to sort it, or use Filter this table.
  5. Use Expand all and Collapse all to open or close every card.

Good to know

  • Nights come from each scout's camping log in Scoutbook, the same total shown on their profile, with pack and personal entries included.
  • Fix Trips to double-check in Scoutbook first. Day visitors can legitimately have 0 nights; for everyone else it means the nights were never entered.
  • The goal box also drives the Overview tile, but always uses 20 nights.
  • Trips from changes the trip counts, the buttons and the trip lists on the cards. The last two columns of the table ignore it.
  • If a scout is missing from a trip's roster in Scoutbook, the trip shows Not in their book until it is added there.

Signed Off Last 90 Days

A running log of the rank and merit badge requirements that were recently signed off in Scoutbook, newest first, with the scouts who got each one. Use it to see what has happened since you last looked, to notice batch entries, and to check a scout's recent work.

How to use it

  1. Leave Last (days) at 90, or type a smaller number. 7 gives a weekly recap. The box will not accept more days than the data covers.
  2. Narrow the list with Search (a requirement, rank, badge or scout), Type (rank requirements or merit badge requirements) and Scout. Any change takes you back to the first page of results.
  3. Read the four cards (marker 1) for the size of the window, then scan the table from the newest date down.
  4. Click a column title to sort. Date Recorded and Scouts start with the biggest or newest first; Type and Requirement start A to Z. Click the same title again to reverse it.
  5. Use the page buttons (marker 5) to move through long lists.

Good to know

  • Date Recorded is the day the sign-off was entered in Scoutbook. When a scout did the work 4 or more days earlier, their name shows done with the earlier date, so late entries are easy to spot.
  • Many scouts on one date, or a high on the busiest day count, usually means a leader entered a batch.
  • Sort by Scouts to find the requirements that were signed off for many scouts at once, for example after a meeting activity.
  • Merit badge sign-offs only go back as far as the data window shown in the page's introduction.
  • The Overview strip "signed off in 30 days (and 90)" counts the same records.

COH Order

Helps you prepare for a Court of Honor. Enter the date of your last Court of Honor and the page lists, scout by scout, every rank and merit badge earned since then. You can sort the list, open each scout to see the dates, and send the whole list to Excel.

How to use it

  1. Type or pick the Court of Honor date: the date of your last ceremony.
  2. Read the three cards, then choose an order with the sort buttons: Scout (A to Z), Rank(s) Completed or # of MBs Completed.
  3. Click a scout's card, or Expand all, to see every rank and merit badge with its date.
  4. Click Download Excel to save a workbook, or Copy for Excel and paste into a spreadsheet (click a cell and press Ctrl+V). The message under the buttons confirms what happened.

Good to know

  • The date you enter is included. If the items from that day were already presented, type the next day instead.
  • Ranks use the date earned in Scoutbook. Merit badges use the day the badge was completed, which can be earlier than the day it was entered. A badge completed before your date but entered later will not be listed.
  • The Excel file has three tabs: Advancements (one row per rank or badge with the scout, what was earned, the type and the date), plus Rank Qty and MB Qty, which count how many of each rank and each merit badge were earned.
  • If the dashboard is open inside another site, such as the OneDrive viewer, the browser may block the download. Copy for Excel still works there, or open the dashboard file directly in your browser.
  • Nothing is saved: the date has to be entered again after you reload the page.

This Week's Meeting

Turns everyone's open requirements into a plan for this week's troop meeting: which scouts to hold a Scoutmaster conference or board of review for first, which stations to run in the time you have, and which waiting-period requirements to start now.

How to use it

  1. Set Program time to the minutes you really have for advancement at this meeting.
  2. Open Who is coming? and tap the names of scouts who are away. They drop out of the plan and the numbers. Everyone and Nobody reset the whole list.
  3. Optional: turn on Pace awareness to favor scouts who are over the troop's typical pace.
  4. Read the summary and the cards, then run the plan: first the conferences and boards under Hold These First, then the Recommended Stations in order. Each station card lists the scouts to pull in and how to run it.
  5. Use Scouts Closest To Their Next Rank to see where each scout stands after the meeting (ready now, ready after this meeting, or needs more), and filter it by scout, next rank or status.
  6. Check Requirements To Focus On for the requirements that help the most scouts, and Start These Clocks This Week for requirements that take days, weeks or months to complete.

Good to know

  • Ready means only the Scoutmaster conference, the board of review, Scout spirit or the parent exercises are left.
  • The plan assumes everyone is here until you change it, and it uses the same open requirements as the other pages. Attendance and settings are not saved; they reset when you reload.
  • With Pace awareness on, scouts who are over the pace count double and scouts at pace risk count one and a half times. It never changes who is ready. The pace statuses are the ones on .
  • The stations come from a list of troop-meeting activities of 10 to 60 minutes each. The Overview reuses this plan for its "ready for conference or board" tile and its meeting panel.
  • If no station helps the scouts you selected, try more program time or add scouts back.

Advancement Groups

Suggests groups of scouts who still need the same requirements, so one session can move several scouts forward at once. There are two separate sets: groups for a troop meeting and groups for a camping trip. Only scouts who have not yet earned First Class are included.

How to use it

  1. Read the cards at the top: scouts not yet at First Class, the number of troop meeting groups and camping trip groups (with how many scouts each set places), and the scouts left out.
  2. Open the group cards under At a troop meeting and On a camping trip. Each card gives a theme, about how long it takes, The plan (steps to run), the scouts in the group, and the requirements it can cover.
  3. If scouts are left out because a group is "already full", raise Largest group (8, 10, 12 or No limit).
  4. Tick Include swimming and boating only if you have a pool or waterfront. It adds a waterfront theme to the camping groups.
  5. Click a scout's name to open their Scout Detail, hover a requirement number to read the requirement, and open Wording and who needs each requirement for the full text.
  6. Check the boxes headed Left out of the troop meeting groups and Left out of the camping trip groups. Each scout there has the reason they did not fit.

Good to know

  • A scout is in at most one group in each set, so the same scout can be in one group at meetings and a different one on a campout.
  • Each set has at most 4 groups (fewer when everyone fits), and every group has at least 2 scouts who share an open requirement.
  • Every open requirement from Scout through First Class counts. Requirements for a scout's next rank count the most, the following rank less, later ranks least. Group 1 is the best-scoring group.
  • Scoutmaster conferences, boards of review and the parent exercises are not group activities, so they are left out.
  • Groups are worked out live from the current data and are never saved.

Advancement Trends

Shows how long scouts take between ranks, how many ranks the troop earns each quarter, and which scouts are behind the troop's typical pace. Use it to spot slowdowns early and to see the troop's long-term pattern.

How to use it

  1. Start with the tiles at the top, then read Time in current rank vs the troop's typical step: each scout's days since their latest rank, next to the troop's median for that step.
  2. Use the six filters (Scout, Latest rank, Working toward, Status, Next rank done, Last entry) and the column titles to sort. The table starts with the scouts furthest over the pace.
  3. Scroll down for the charts: average time between ranks, the last 10 scouts to reach First Class, ranks earned per quarter, the pace of each class of new scouts, and merit badges earned.
  4. Hover over a bar to see its exact numbers.

Good to know

  • Over the pace means longer than the troop's median for that step. Pace risk means within 30 days before the median, or exactly at it. Within pace means earlier than that. No comparison means there is no median for the step or the scout has no rank yet.
  • Days are counted to the date in the header (when the data was pulled), not to today, and the Last entry column ignores Book Checked marks, so it can differ from .
  • The Last entry colors use the yellow and red limits you set on Rank Update Aging (30 and 90 days at first).
  • Setting Status to Over the pace and Last entry to Stale (red) finds slow scouts that nobody is updating. Working toward First Class or below matches the early-rank tile.
  • Steps longer than 3 years are left out of the averages. Merit badge bars follow the date badges were recorded, so entering many at once makes a spike. The class table only counts scouts who reached First Class, so recent classes look faster than they will end up.
  • Dates come from the date earned in Scoutbook. Ranks without a date are left out.
